lessons.title: Hello, Rust

answers: It returns a Result the caller has to handle
It is a macro, expanded into code before compilation
It writes to stderr rather than stdout
writing.exampleCaption: The captured name fills the {name} placeholder. Rust checks that formatting expression during compilation; the resulting line appears on stdout when the program runs.
writing.explanation:
A Rust executable begins in `fn` main(). The braces enclose the statements that run when the program starts. In the example, name is a string slice, and `println!`("Hello, {name}!") uses it to build a line of text. The exclamation mark matters: `println!` is a macro, not an ordinary function call. It expands while the program is compiled, so the compiler can check the format string and its arguments before anything runs. If a placeholder is missing an argument, you see a diagnostic instead of a half-working program.

Follow the diagram from left to right: source code, a successful compile-time check, then terminal output. The compiler’s messages are not the same as your program’s stdout. A clean build can still produce no output if there is no print call; a failed build cannot run this new version at all. When you change the greeting, predict the exact line you expect before tapping Run. Then compare that prediction with the actual output, including punctuation and spaces. This edit–compile–run–observe cycle is the habit you will use throughout the course.

Start with the three places where text can appear. Your source file contains instructions; the compiler may report an error while checking those instructions; the running program may print a line to standard output. These are separate events. For this example, a successful compile produces a program, and running that program prints exactly `Hello, Crabrix!` followed by a newline. The code does not display a window or return that greeting as the function's value. `println!` writes it to the output stream.

Read the punctuation slowly. `fn` begins a function declaration, `main` is the entry point, `()` says it takes no parameters, and `{ ... }` surrounds its body. `let name = "Crabrix";` creates a binding. The semicolon ends that statement. Inside the quoted format string, `{name}` asks formatting to read the binding. Removing the exclamation mark changes the syntax into a call to a function named `println`, which this program has not defined. Removing the argument or misspelling the captured name causes a compile error. Neither mistake means that a previous successful run printed something new.

Try one change at a time so the cause stays visible. First change only `Crabrix` to your name and predict the line. Then change `Hello` to `Welcome` and predict again. Finally make the format string refer to an unknown binding and read the compiler's primary diagnostic. Restore the code after that experiment. If the output surprises you, check which source version you actually built, whether compilation succeeded, and whether you are reading compiler messages or program output.
writing.feedback: The exclamation mark marks a macro invocation. `println!` expands at compile time, allowing Rust to check its format string and supplied values before execution.
writing.question: Why does `println!` end with an exclamation mark?
writing.rule: Execution begins in `fn` main(). `println!` is a compile-time-checked macro that writes a formatted line to stdout when the program runs.
writing.success: The program exits with code 0 and stdout contains the greeting you predicted. After the deliberately broken placeholder, the compiler identifies the formatting mistake instead of producing new stdout.
writing.summary: A small Rust program gives you the whole development loop: write a function, `let` the compiler check it, run it, and inspect what appeared on stdout.
writing.task: Change the greeting and the name, then write down the exact output you predict. Run the project and compare stdout with your prediction. Try a mismatched format placeholder and notice that compilation stops before a new program runs.

lessons.title: Variables

answers: 5 and 6 are different types
value is immutable without mut
Numbers cannot be reassigned
writing.exampleCaption: Shadowing makes a new binding; `mut` changes an existing one.
writing.exampleCode:
let total = 10;        // immutable
let total = total + 5; // shadowed
let mut counter = 0;   // mutable
counter += 1;
writing.explanation:
Start by reading each `let` as a promise about one binding. In `let total = 10`, the name `total` cannot be reassigned. The next line, `let total = total + 5`, does not change that first binding: the right side reads its value, then a new binding with the same name hides it. This is shadowing. It is useful when data passes through a clear transformation, such as trimming text and then parsing it, because the name can follow the meaning of the value even when its type changes.

Mutation is a different promise. `let mut counter = 0` permits `counter += 1` to update one existing binding. Choose `mut` when the same piece of state evolves over time, such as a counter in a loop; choose shadowing when a new stage of computation replaces the old view. Neither choice makes every value in the program mutable. Try removing `mut` and read the compiler error, then try replacing the update with a new `let counter = counter + 1`. Compare which version better communicates your intent to the next reader.

A useful test is to put a transformation at the same scope and ask whether the earlier form should still be available. Shadowing hides that earlier binding under the reused name; it does not mutate memory by magic. In a nested block, a shadowed name can stop hiding the outer one when the block ends. This is why naming and scope matter as much as the presence of `mut`.

Think of a binding as a name attached to a value, not a box that must change. `let score = 3;` creates an immutable binding by default. A later assignment to that same binding needs `let mut score = 3;` at the declaration. This rule helps you see which parts of a program can change while it runs. It does not mean all underlying data in Rust is forever fixed; it describes what this binding permits.

Shadowing is different from assignment. A second `let score = ...;` starts a new binding with the same name. The old value is no longer reachable by that name in the new scope, and the new value can even have a different type. An assignment such as `score = ...;` keeps the same binding and must respect its type. Trace each `let` in the example with a small table: line, name, value, type, and whether later assignment is permitted. That table is more useful than memorizing that one syntax is 'mutable' and the other is not.

Try making a counter with `mut` and increment it twice. Predict the final printed value. Then rewrite the same calculation using a new shadowing `let` for each step. Finally attempt to assign text to a numeric mutable binding and read the type error. If a name appears in a nested block, mark where that block starts and ends; a shadowing binding exists only within its scope. These experiments prepare you for ownership: Rust tracks not just what a value is, but which binding may use it at each point.
writing.feedback: Add `mut`, or shadow with a second `let` if a new binding is what you meant.
writing.practiceCode:
let value = 5;
value = 6;
writing.question: Why is the reassignment rejected?
writing.rule: `mut` permits mutation; shadowing replaces the binding entirely.
writing.success: The final program compiles without an unnecessary-`mut` warning. You can point to the new binding created by shadowing and to the single existing binding updated through `mut`.
writing.summary: A binding names a value. Rust keeps that binding fixed by default, asks for `mut` when the value must change, and uses a fresh `let` when you want to shadow it.
writing.task: Create an immutable value, shadow it with a transformed value, and update one mutable counter. Predict which names can be reassigned before compiling; then remove `mut` once and explain the diagnostic.

answers: Only after the user sees stdout
While println! expands during compilation

writing.exampleCaption: Names can be captured directly inside a checked format string.
writing.explanation:
`println!` takes a format string and turns values into a line on stdout. In the example, `{name}` and `{builds}` capture bindings with those names. The macro checks the placeholders while compiling, so a misspelled capture or missing positional argument becomes a diagnostic before the program runs. This is safer than assembling a message with a chain of ad hoc string additions, especially when the output becomes a log line or a table someone else must read.

Formatting controls presentation without changing the stored value. In `{builds:>3}`, the colon introduces a format specification: `>` right-aligns the value in a field three characters wide. With `builds = 4`, that line begins with two spaces and then 4. Predict the whitespace rather than relying on how a proportional font looks. Try replacing a named capture with `{}` and pass the value explicitly; then remove the argument and observe how rustc identifies the mismatch. Use formatting to communicate, but keep business decisions outside the format string so the data and its display remain easy to reason about.

A placeholder also asks the value to support the requested formatting trait. Ordinary `{}` output uses `Display`, while `{:?}` is a `Debug` view often useful during inspection. If a custom type has no suitable implementation, rustc reports that requirement rather than inventing a representation. The width in `:>3` is a minimum, not a maximum: a longer number is not truncated. Use that rule to predict both a one-digit and a four-digit count before running.

A format string is a template. Literal characters appear in output exactly as written, while each placeholder is replaced with a formatted value. `{}` consumes a positional argument; `{name}` can capture a named local binding. The compiler checks that placeholders and supplied arguments agree. A second `{}` without a second value is a compile-time mistake, not a blank that Rust fills automatically.

Formatting also changes how a value is represented. `{value}` uses `Display`, which aims at a reader-friendly form; `{value:?}` uses `Debug`, which is often useful while investigating program state. `Some` types implement one but not the other. `println!` appends a newline after formatting; `print!` does not. An escaped brace is written `{{` or `}}` when you want a literal brace in the output. Spaces and punctuation inside the quotes are ordinary data, so write down the expected line character by character before running.

Build a tiny receipt line from a label and a number. First use positional placeholders, then use captured names. Add a literal pair of braces and compare the result. Next deliberately remove one argument and identify the compiler message before repairing it. For an unexpected output, distinguish three questions: did it compile, did the program run, and did the format string contain exactly the characters you intended? This habit prevents a surprising amount of debugging by guesswork.
writing.feedback: `println!` is a macro, so malformed placeholders become compiler errors.
writing.practiceCode:
let language = "Rust";
println!("Learning {language}");
writing.question: When is the format string checked?
writing.rule: Every formatting placeholder must have a value known to `println!`.
writing.success: stdout contains the expected words and alignment; the malformed positional call fails at compile time. You can explain which placeholder consumed each value.
writing.summary: A format string is a checked template: each placeholder has a value, and the finished line follows the template exactly, including spaces and alignment.
writing.task: Print a name and build count on one line, then right-align the count to width three on the next. Record the exact spaces you expect. Switch one capture to {} and deliberately omit its argument once.

lessons.title: Numbers

answers: Rust cannot add integers
u32 and i32 are distinct types
Only usize supports addition
writing.exampleCaption: The annotations document three different jobs.
writing.explanation:
Integers and floating-point values model different kinds of information. A signed integer such as `i32` can represent negative values; an unsigned type such as `u8` uses its bits for nonnegative values. `usize` is the natural type for an index or collection length because it matches the platform’s address width. f64 represents a broad range of fractional values, but most decimal fractions are approximations in binary, so exact equality is often the wrong test for a measured quantity. `None` of these types is automatically better: start with what the domain means.

In the example, files is a length-like count, temperature is fractional, and mask is one byte of bit flags. Those annotations tell a reader why the three values should not be treated as interchangeable. Rust refuses to add unrelated numeric types without a conversion, which forces you to choose the result range and sign deliberately. Before adding a cast, ask whether negative values are possible, whether the result can exceed the smaller type, and whether rounding matters. Try an explicit conversion only after answering those questions; a broad as cast can hide a narrowing mistake rather than solve it.

Type inference still has rules. A bare integer literal commonly defaults to `i32` when nothing else constrains it, and a bare floating literal commonly defaults to f64. An assignment, function parameter, or explicit annotation can provide the needed context. That is why the same literal may be accepted in one place and rejected in another. Read the expected and found types in the diagnostic instead of adding as automatically; a conversion should express a deliberate boundary between numeric domains.

An integer type sets both a range and a representation. `u8` can hold whole numbers from 0 through 255; `i8` includes negative values but has a smaller positive maximum. Types such as `usize` are used for collection indices and sizes and depend on the target pointer width. A floating-point type such as `f64` represents many fractional values approximately, not as exact decimal money. Choose the type from the domain's valid values and operations, not from the smallest spelling.

Rust often infers a type from context, but it does not silently turn every numeric value into whatever a later expression wants. Adding a `u8` to an `i32` requires an explicit decision about conversion. A cast with `as` has defined conversion behavior, but it can truncate or wrap values; use `TryFrom` when out-of-range input should produce an error. Division of two integers discards the fractional part. Overflow behavior also depends on operation and build context, so use checked or saturating operations when the domain needs an explicit policy.

Try computing an average from two whole numbers. Predict the result of integer division, then convert deliberately to floating point and compare. Next parse a value that may exceed `u8` and handle the failed conversion instead of assuming it fits. Write a one-sentence reason for each chosen type. This is the real skill: using a type to state a valid range and deciding what happens at its boundaries.
writing.feedback: Convert deliberately only after deciding which range and sign rule the result needs.
writing.question: Why is the addition rejected?
writing.rule: Numeric conversions are explicit because ranges and precision differ.
writing.success: The values compile with types that match their jobs. You can justify every conversion and identify one situation where a narrowing cast would be `unsafe`.
writing.summary: Choosing a number type records a promise about range and precision. Rust makes conversions explicit so that promise cannot change silently at an arithmetic boundary.
writing.task: Choose types for a file count, a temperature, and one byte of flags. Explain the range or precision each choice needs; then try mixing two types and decide which explicit conversion preserves the intended result.

lessons.title: Booleans

answers: A comparison such as count > 0
count as bool
Nothing; every nonzero integer is true
writing.exampleCaption: The name says what must be true before work starts.
writing.explanation:
A condition is not an arbitrary number or string in Rust. Comparisons such as builds > 0 and errors == 0 each produce a `bool`. The example combines them into ready, a name that expresses the decision the program needs to make. That makes the if branch easy to inspect: it runs only after at least one build exists and no errors remain. If your code says if count, rustc asks for a real boolean condition instead of guessing whether zero should mean false.

The logical operators also control which work is performed. For left && right, a false left side settles the answer, so right is not evaluated. For left || right, a true left side settles it. This is short-circuiting, shown in the diagram by the crossed-out right branch. It matters when the right expression is expensive or valid only after the left has checked a precondition. Do not use side effects on the right merely because you expect them to run: the operator may skip them. Predict the result for each pair of boolean values, then use ! to reverse one condition and check that the branch still says what you intend.

You can use short-circuiting as a safe guard, for example checking that an index is in range before reading an element on the right side of &&. Reverse the order and the protection disappears. Parentheses help when a condition mixes && and ||: write the grouping you mean instead of making a future reader remember precedence. A descriptive name such as ready often makes the decision clearer than repeating the whole expression at every if.

A boolean has exactly two values: `true` and `false`. A comparison such as `age >= 18` produces a boolean; an `if` condition requires one. Rust does not treat `0`, an empty string, or a null pointer as false. That explicitness makes the meaning of a branch visible. Use `==` to compare and `=` to assign; confusing them produces a compiler diagnostic rather than a silent change of logic.

`&&` means both conditions must be true. `||` means at least one must be true. They short-circuit: for `left && right`, Rust skips `right` if `left` is false; for `left || right`, it skips `right` if `left` is true. This matters when the right side is expensive or could be invalid without the left-side guard. For example, check that a collection is nonempty before accessing a first element. Parentheses can make a mixed expression easier to read even when precedence rules would choose the same grouping.

Draw a two-column truth table for two conditions such as `has_ticket` and `is_open`. Predict the result of `has_ticket && is_open` for all four input pairs. Then change `&&` to `||` and explain which rows changed. Finally put a visible print in the right-hand expression and observe when it is skipped. If the result surprises you, evaluate each comparison first, then combine the booleans; do not reason from the English sentence alone.
writing.feedback: Write the condition you mean explicitly, such as count > 0.
writing.question: What must replace count in the condition?
writing.rule: if requires `bool`; Rust has no implicit numeric truthiness.
writing.success: The branch runs only for the intended combination of values. You can explain why each skipped right-hand expression was unnecessary.
writing.summary: A comparison produces a `bool`, and a branch requires one. && and || can skip their right-hand expression as soon as the result is known.
writing.task: Build a clearly named condition from two comparisons. Predict whether the right side of && runs when the left is false, and whether the right side of || runs when the left is true.

lessons.title: Characters & Text

answers: Visible symbols
UTF-8 bytes
Words
writing.exampleCaption: The crab is one `char` but several UTF-8 bytes.
writing.explanation:
Single quotes construct a `char`, while double quotes construct text. A `char` is one Unicode scalar value, not necessarily one byte. The crab emoji in the example fits in one `char` but occupies several UTF-8 bytes. `&str` is a borrowed view of UTF-8 text; its `len()` reports bytes. If you ask for `chars().count()`, you count scalar values instead. A user-perceived character can contain more than one scalar, such as a letter plus a combining mark, so even that count is not a universal measure of what a person sees.

Rust does not allow `s[0]` on a string because byte position zero is not a safe general-purpose character index. Instead, choose the operation that matches the question: `bytes()` when inspecting the encoding, `chars()` when processing scalars, and a grapheme-aware library when the interface needs visible clusters. This distinction prevents slicing through a multibyte UTF-8 sequence. Try printing the byte length and scalar count for plain ASCII and for the crab emoji. Predict both numbers before running, then compare them with the output and explain why they differ.

Consider the visible letter é. It can be stored as one scalar or as e followed by a combining accent; those forms can look the same while having different byte and scalar counts. That is why text handling should start from the user question, not from a convenient index. Byte length is useful for storage and protocols, scalar iteration for some parsing tasks, and grapheme clusters for many cursor and selection operations.

A Rust `char` is one Unicode scalar value, written with single quotes such as `'é'`. A string slice `&str` is text encoded as UTF-8 bytes. A visible character can require more than one scalar value: a letter plus a combining accent or a family emoji may be multiple scalars even though a reader sees one symbol. This is why 'character count' needs a definition before you write the code.

ASCII letters use one UTF-8 byte, while many other scalars use several. `text.len()` returns byte length, not a count of visible symbols. `text.chars().count()` counts Unicode scalar values, which is still not always a count of what a person sees. Indexing a string by an arbitrary number could point into the middle of a multibyte encoding, so Rust does not provide `text[0]` as a universal character operation. Iterating over `chars()` or using a byte slice with checked boundaries makes the choice explicit.

Use a short ASCII word, one accented character, and one emoji. For each, predict `len()` and `chars().count()` before running. Then try to take a byte slice across a UTF-8 boundary and observe that an invalid boundary is rejected at runtime. A production UI may need a Unicode grapheme-segmentation library to count user-perceived characters. For learning, state whether your algorithm cares about bytes, scalar values, or visible graphemes; the right answer depends on the task.
writing.feedback: Use `text.chars().count()` when Unicode scalar values are the unit you need.
writing.practiceCode:
let text = "🦀";
println!("{}", text.len());
writing.question: What does `len()` report for `&str`?
writing.rule: `String` indexing by an arbitrary byte is forbidden because UTF-8 boundaries matter.
writing.success: Your prediction matches the output, and you can say which counting method answers which question without treating bytes as visible characters.
writing.summary: Rust text has several useful units: bytes for encoding, Unicode scalar values for `char`, and sometimes multiple scalars for one visible symbol.
writing.task: Print a `char` and a borrowed string, then compare `len()` with `chars().count()` for ASCII and an emoji. Predict the byte and scalar counts before running.

lessons.title: Reading rustc

answers: The primary source span and expected/found pair
The final warning in the file
Any suggested cast, applied automatically
writing.exampleCaption: The annotation creates an expected type rustc can compare.
writing.explanation:
When rustc rejects a program, begin at the highlighted source span. The message usually names what type was expected and what expression was actually found. In the example, count is annotated `u32`, while "four" is text; the compiler cannot turn that word into an unsigned integer by guessing. The primary span points to the conflicting value. Nearby labels and notes explain how the expectation was established, and a help message may suggest an operation. Treat suggestions as evidence, not commands: first decide what the program should mean.

If the count should be four, replace the text with the numeric literal 4. If the user really supplies text, parsing is a separate, fallible step that returns a `Result` and needs error handling. Those are different programs. Fix the earliest causal mismatch and compile again before chasing a long list of later messages; one root error can make downstream expressions appear broken. The diagram shows a different type mismatch but the same reading order: locate the span, compare types, choose a conversion only if it preserves intent, then recheck the build.

Compiler messages often include a code such as E0308 and a help suggestion. The code is useful for looking up the rule, while the span tells you where this particular program violates it. A suggestion to parse text may compile only after you handle the possibility of invalid input; adding unwrap just to silence a diagnostic changes the failure mode to a runtime panic. Prefer a fix you can explain in terms of the data the program actually has.

A compiler error is evidence about a particular source version. First confirm that the file you edited is the one being built. Then read the primary error message and its highlighted span before looking at follow-up notes. 'Expected' and 'found' describe a disagreement the compiler can point to, but the best fix may be earlier than the underlined token. One missing delimiter can produce many later diagnostics; repair the first meaningful error and rebuild before chasing the rest.

Do not treat a compiler suggestion as an instruction to apply mechanically. Ask what your program is meant to do. If Rust suggests borrowing instead of moving a value, decide whether the function truly needs ownership or only temporary access. If it suggests a conversion, decide what should happen when the input is out of range. Compiler feedback is strongest when combined with a prediction about the intended data flow.

Create three controlled errors: a misspelled variable, a wrong argument type, and a missing brace. For each, record the first error category, the line and column, and the smallest intentional edit that repairs the program. Rebuild after each fix. Compare the failed build with a successful run: diagnostics describe why a new program was not produced, while stdout comes from a program that did run. That distinction keeps the learning loop precise even when the interface shows compiler messages and output near one another.

lessons.title: Compound Types

answers: It compiles and panics at runtime with an index error
The compiler rejects an index it can prove is out of range
It wraps around to the first element like a ring buffer
writing.exampleCaption: Position for a tuple, index for an array.
writing.explanation:
Tuples group a fixed number of possibly different types and are read by position. Arrays hold one type with a length known at compile time, which is exactly what lets the compiler bounds-check them and reject an out-of-range index it can see.

The point in the example is a tuple: its first field is an `i32` and its second is an f64. The fields are read as point.0 and point.1 because their positions, not names, identify them. The scores array is different: all four elements are `u8`, and the length 4 belongs to the type [`u8`; 4]. That makes `scores[2]` a predictable access to the third score. Before using an index, ask whether the index is a constant the compiler can reject or a runtime value that needs a check.

Tuples help when a few values belong together for a short journey through code. Arrays help when you have a fixed-size sequence of one kind of item. Neither is a general substitute for a struct with meaningful field names or a `Vec` that must grow. Choosing the shape is part of explaining the data, not merely satisfying syntax. In a function signature, (`i32`, f64) tells callers exactly what comes back, while [`u8`; 4] promises exactly four scores.

Try changing the tuple field order and observe which accesses now need a different type. Then change the array length annotation without changing its elements. Compare the two diagnostics: one concerns the type at a position, the other concerns the number of elements. Predict whether an out-of-range constant index will be caught before execution, and distinguish that case from an index read from user input.

A type annotation can document intent at a public boundary or resolve an otherwise ambiguous parse. Inside a small expression, inference usually keeps the code lighter. Add annotations where they help the reader or compiler choose, not mechanically to every binding.

A type tells the compiler which operations a value supports and how it is represented. `i32` is a signed 32-bit integer, `bool` is true or false, and `&str` is borrowed UTF-8 text. A tuple groups values by position; an array stores a fixed number of values of one element type. Read a type annotation from the inside out instead of trying to memorize every symbol at once. For `[i32; 3]`, the element type is `i32` and the length is three.

Inference works when the surrounding code gives enough information, but an explicit annotation can document intent or settle ambiguity. Try changing a tuple element from a number to text and see which later operations stop compiling. Then compare an array with a `Vec`: an array's length is part of its type, while a vector can grow. When a type error appears, find the expression that produces the value and the place that expects it. The difference between those two is the decision you need to make.
writing.feedback: A constant index past a known length is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.

let value = items[5];
writing.question: What happens with that index?
writing.rule: A tuple mixes types by position; an array holds one type with a fixed length.
writing.success: The output shows both values with no type mismatch.
writing.summary: Rust checks scalar and compound types before the program runs.

lessons.title: Operators & Casting

answers: wrapping_add
checked_add
saturating_add
writing.exampleCaption: Say what should happen at the boundary instead of hoping.
writing.explanation:
There is no implicit numeric promotion: adding a `u8` to a `u32` is a compile error until you convert. In a debug build an overflowing add panics rather than silently wrapping, and in release it wraps — which is why the standard library gives you checked_, wrapping_, and saturating_ variants to say which one you meant.

The example shows why an overflow policy must be explicit. A `u8` can hold values from 0 through 255, so 250 + 10 does not fit. checked_add returns `None` rather than a number; wrapping_add cycles around to 4; saturating_add clamps at 255. These are three different product decisions. A count of completed tasks probably should not wrap from 255 to 4, while a circular sequence number may intentionally do so. Pick the behavior from the domain before choosing the method.

The later as cast illustrates another boundary. Converting 300_i32 to `u8` with as keeps only the low eight bits, yielding 44. This is not a harmless way to make two types agree. If narrowing should fail when a value does not fit, use a checked conversion such as `u8::try_from`(big) and handle its `Result`. If the source is known to fit, record why that invariant holds. Rust's refusal to silently promote mixed numeric operands gives you a chance to make that reasoning visible.

Overflow checking can be configured, so avoid depending on a debug-versus-release difference as part of program logic. The named arithmetic methods communicate behavior reliably in either build. As an exercise, write the expected output for all three additions before running the example, then explain which one would be appropriate for a byte-sized inventory counter that must report an error when it exceeds its limit.

Do not assume all numeric conversions happen automatically. Rust requires deliberate casts where types differ, and a cast can truncate or change meaning. Start with concrete types, then inspect the compiler diagnostic before changing them to make an expression compile.

Operators are short names for operations, but their result still has a type and a range. Integer division truncates toward zero; `%` returns a remainder. A comparison returns `bool`, not a number. If several operators appear in one expression, add parentheses while learning so you can see exactly which operation happens first. The compiler can catch incompatible operands, but it cannot tell you whether the formula itself matches the problem.

Try calculating the cost of three items after a discount. Write the steps as separate bindings, print each intermediate value, and compare with a single expression. Then test a boundary such as zero divisor or a value near the maximum of your integer type. Decide whether your program should reject, clamp, or explicitly handle that case. Converting between numeric types is a policy decision: a cast that silently loses information may be wrong even if it compiles.
writing.feedback: checked_* returns `Option`, so the caller decides what an overflow means.
writing.question: Which call returns `None` instead of panicking or wrapping?
writing.rule: Rust never converts numeric types for you, and overflow is a decision you make by name.
writing.success: The program compiles and the boundary case is handled explicitly.
writing.summary: Arithmetic in Rust is checked, and conversions are always written down.
writing.task: Pick the right overflow strategy for a counter that must never wrap.

lessons.title: Block Expressions

answers: bool
writing.exampleCaption: The final multiplication becomes the value of the block.
writing.explanation:
Most Rust syntax is expression-oriented. The last expression in a block becomes its value when it has no semicolon. Adding a semicolon changes that expression into a statement and the block then produces (), the unit value. This one rule explains function returns, if branches, match arms, and scoped calculations.

Read the braces as a small computation with its own scope. In the example, base exists inside the block, then base * 2 is the final expression. The whole block evaluates to 14, which is assigned to score. There is no separate return statement because the final expression supplies the value. If you put a semicolon after base * 2, that line becomes a statement and the block's value becomes (), the unit type. A variable expecting an integer can no longer receive it.

This rule appears repeatedly in Rust. A function body may end with a value, each branch of an if expression may produce a value, and each match arm may do the same. The pattern lets control flow and data flow stay close together. It also makes scope useful: temporary names can exist only while the value is being computed. A block can be clear and focused; it should not hide a long sequence of unrelated side effects just to produce one final number.

Try assigning a block to a variable with an explicit `i32` annotation. First return an integer, then add the accidental semicolon and read the expected-versus-found message. Next create two nested blocks and name which variables remain visible after each closing brace. The closing brace ends the scope; the last unsuffixed expression determines the value that escapes it.

In Rust, a block can do work and then produce a value. The final expression has no trailing semicolon when you want its value to leave the block. Add a semicolon and the block instead yields the unit value `()`. That tiny punctuation mark often explains an `expected i32, found ()` error. An `if` expression follows the same idea: each branch must produce a compatible type when the whole `if` is used as a value.

Trace a block with two `let` statements and one final calculation. Mark which lines are statements and which expression supplies the result. Next use an `if` expression to choose a label based on a score. Deliberately add a semicolon to one branch's final expression and read the compiler's type comparison. If a block is not supposed to produce a meaningful value, ending its statements with semicolons is normal. The rule is about what the surrounding code expects.
writing.feedback: The semicolon discards the numeric value, leaving the block's unit value.
writing.question: What type does value have?
writing.rule: No semicolon means a tail value; a semicolon turns it into ().
writing.success: The binding receives the tail expression's numeric value.
writing.summary: A block can perform statements and then produce one final value.
writing.task: Calculate a value inside a block and return it without return.

The semicolon discards the value, so it returns ()
The parameters must be declared mut to be read twice
writing.exampleCaption: The final expression is the result — no `return` keyword needed.
writing.explanation:
Parameter types and the return type are always written out, never inferred across a function boundary. The last expression is the return value when you leave the semicolon off, which is why an accidental semicolon turns a function into one that returns the unit type and produces a type error.

The area function declares its contract before its body: two `u32` parameters go in and one `u32` comes out. That boundary lets rustc check a call without reading every line of the implementation. Inside the body, width * height is the tail expression. Its value becomes the return value because there is no semicolon after it. Adding one would change that final statement to unit, and rustc would point out the mismatch with -> `u32`.

The shout function shows that a body can have several steps before its tail value. text is borrowed as `&str`, to_uppercase creates an owned `String`, and push modifies that owned buffer. The final out expression moves the completed `String` to the caller. The function does not return a reference to its local buffer, which would be invalid after the call. A signature is therefore also a useful hint about ownership: `&str` is borrowed input, `String` is an owned result.

When writing a new function, start with the inputs and result you want a caller to see. Then use a small example call to test that contract. If two branches can return different kinds of value, resolve that design rather than hoping inference will cross the function boundary. Predict the type of each tail expression, and compare it with the declared return type before compiling.

A function name should describe the guarantee it gives, while the signature makes the input and output types checkable. Keep the body focused enough that a reader can predict its result before scrolling. Test a normal value and an edge case; if the latter is ambiguous, specify the behavior in the contract.

A function gives one operation a name and a boundary. Parameters are inputs chosen by the caller; the declared return type tells callers what comes back. A function body returns its final expression unless it uses an explicit `return`. Printing inside a function and returning a value are different effects. A caller can use a returned number in another expression; printed text is already sent to stdout and is not the function's return value.

Take the sample function and write down one row for each call: argument values, parameter bindings, calculated result, and any printed line. Change a parameter type and see which call sites fail to compile. Then remove the trailing semicolon from a final expression or add one to witness the return-type error. Prefer a small function with a clear name over copying the same calculation in several places. If you cannot describe the function in one sentence, its responsibility may be too broad.
writing.feedback: A trailing semicolon turns an expression into a statement, and the function then returns ().
writing.question: Why does that function fail to compile?
writing.rule: The last expression without a semicolon is the return value.
writing.success: It compiles with no `return` keyword and the type matches the signature.
writing.summary: A function signature is a contract the compiler enforces at every call site.

answers: The argument is &str but the parameter is u32
A literal has to be bound to a variable first
double must return the same type it accepts
writing.exampleCaption: Both inputs and the output are visible before reading the body.
writing.explanation:
Rust requires every parameter type to be written, which lets the body and every call be checked independently. Arguments are the concrete values passed at a call site; parameters are the named inputs in the definition. Passing an owned type may move it, while a reference lets the function borrow it — a distinction later lessons develop in depth.

In `fn` area(width: `u32`, height: `u32`), width and height are parameters: names the function uses inside its body. In area(4, 3), 4 and 3 are arguments: values supplied by one call. Rust checks that each argument can be used as the corresponding declared type. A literal often gains its type from this context, so you do not have to bind 4 to a separate `u32` variable before calling area.

Order matters even when types match. area(4, 3) and area(3, 4) happen to return the same number, but a function such as subtract(left, right) would not. Choose parameter names that tell the reader which role each value plays, and use a struct when a call would otherwise contain many similar-looking arguments. The body can then focus on computation, while the signature communicates the input contract to every caller.

The ownership aspect becomes more important with non-Copy values. Passing a `String` by value normally transfers ownership to the function; passing `&str` lets it borrow text for reading. At this stage, inspect the parameter type rather than assuming a call always copies. Add a third argument to area and read the arity diagnostic, then pass text where a `u32` is expected and compare that type diagnostic. Each points to a different part of the same contract.

Try calling the function twice with the same `String`. If the first call owns its parameter, the second call exposes the move clearly. Change the parameter to `&str` when reading is enough, then pass both a string literal and a borrowed `String` to verify the flexible interface.

At a call site, arguments must match the function's parameter types and order. A function that accepts `&str` borrows text; one that accepts `String` takes ownership of a growable string. This affects what the caller can do afterward. The signature is therefore more than documentation: it is an enforceable contract about both values and ownership.

For each parameter in the example, label whether the function reads it, mutates through it, or owns it. If it only needs to read a string, try passing a borrowed `&str` instead of moving a `String`. Then try swapping two same-typed arguments and notice that the compiler cannot catch a semantic mix-up just because their types match. Named domain types or a small struct can make such calls safer. When designing a function, choose the least ownership it needs and make the result or error explicit.
writing.feedback: The call site must provide the `u32` promised by the parameter type.
writing.question: Why is the call rejected?
writing.rule: Parameters need explicit types; arguments must satisfy them.
writing.success: The signature communicates exactly which values enter and leave.
writing.summary: A function signature is a compact contract for every caller.

lessons.title: Control Flow

answers: The condition must be an integer, not a bool
The branches produce different types
An if expression cannot be bound with let
writing.exampleCaption: if is an expression, so both arms must agree on a type.
writing.explanation:
Because if is an expression, both branches must produce the same type — there is no silent conversion to paper over a mismatch. loop, while, and for then express three different repetition rules: forever, until a condition fails, and over an iterator.

In the example, value % 2 == 0 evaluates to `bool`. Both if branches produce a `&str`, so the entire if expression can initialize label. If one branch returned a number instead, rustc would reject the assignment because a single expression cannot have two unrelated result types. This is a useful discipline: deciding what label means happens in one place, and the loop can simply print it.

The range 0..3 supplies 0, 1, and 2 to for. Each iteration binds index to the next value and prints one line. The loop does not need a separate counter mutation or a manual exit condition. Later you will see while for a condition that changes over time and loop for cases where break itself decides when to stop. Here, for expresses the finite sequence directly.

A match expression can provide the same kind of value selection when there are more than two cases. Every arm must be covered, and all arms used as one expression must agree on a result type. Predict the three output lines before running, including their order. Then change one branch from "even" to 0 and explain the diagnostic in terms of the type of label, rather than treating it as an arbitrary compiler restriction.

One subtlety is that `if let` is attractive for a single interesting shape, while `match` makes every alternative explicit. If a branch is used as a value, confirm that all paths produce the same type before deciding where the semicolon belongs. Test the boundary condition itself, not only values comfortably on either side.

An `if` chooses a branch from a boolean condition; `match` checks which pattern a value has; loops repeat work. Rust does not guess whether a number or string should count as true. This makes the decision visible at the line where it happens. When an `if` supplies a value, both branches must agree on a type. When it only performs side effects, returning `()` is fine.

Trace the sample with at least two different inputs. For each, write the condition's value, the branch selected, and the value produced. Then replace a long chain of related conditions with `match` and ask whether all cases are covered. The compiler helps check exhaustive matches, but it cannot decide whether your branch rule is the one a user expects. Put boundary inputs in your examples: equal to a threshold, one below it, and one above it. Most mistakes in a branch are at those boundaries.
writing.feedback: An if expression has one type, so every branch has to match.

writing.question: Why do those two branches not type-check?
writing.rule: if is an expression; every branch must produce the same type.
writing.success: Each number prints once with the right classification.
writing.summary: Expressions and loops model decisions without hidden coercion.

lessons.title: Ranges

writing.exampleCaption: The two ranges have different upper-bound rules.
writing.explanation:
The range 0..3 contains 0, 1, and 2; its upper bound is excluded. The inclusive form 1..=3 also contains 3. Half-open ranges fit indexing because a length can be used directly as the excluded end. Inclusive ranges are useful when both endpoints belong to the domain.

Half-open ranges make boundaries compose cleanly. In 0..3, the first value is included and 3 is excluded, so there are exactly three integers. This mirrors a slice whose length is 3: valid positions are 0, 1, and 2, while the length itself is the first position after the slice. Two adjacent spans such as 0..3 and 3..6 meet without overlapping. That is why half-open intervals are common in indexing and iteration.

The inclusive form 1..=3 includes both endpoints and is a natural fit when the domain itself is phrased that way: days one through three, or levels one through three. The syntax is not just decoration. Changing .. to ..= alters which values a for loop sees and may add one more iteration. Write out the sequence before running whenever an off-by-one error would matter.

Ranges are values that can be passed to operations, but the exact kinds they support depend on their element type. A range does not automatically protect every use of its numbers as indexes; you still need to know the collection length. Change the upper bound in the sample to 0..=3 and predict the extra line, then try a zero-length half-open range such as 3..3 and explain why the loop body does not run.

A range communicates which endpoints belong to an operation. `0..n` includes zero and excludes `n`; `0..=n` includes both ends. For a collection of length `n`, valid indices stop at `n - 1`, so `0..n` matches them exactly when `n` is positive. This is one reason half-open ranges appear often in Rust. The type of a range is not a collection of stored numbers; iteration produces the values as needed.

Write the values generated by `2..5` and `2..=5` before running either loop. Then test an empty range such as `3..3` and explain why its body never runs. For indexing, prefer iterating over items directly when you do not need indices; use `enumerate()` when you need both an index and an item. Boundary reasoning matters more than memorizing one syntax: state clearly whether the end is inside or outside the operation.
writing.feedback: The upper bound of .. is excluded, so 5 is not part of the range.
writing.practiceCode: let values: Vec<_> = (2..5).collect();
writing.question: Which values are collected?
writing.rule: a..b excludes b; a..=b includes b.
writing.success: The output has no missing or accidental extra endpoint.
writing.summary: Range syntax makes boundaries visible instead of hiding an off-by-one rule.

writing.explanation:
for consumes an iterator, while repeats while a condition remains true, and loop has no condition at all. A loop expression can return a value with break value. continue skips directly to the next iteration. Selecting the narrowest form makes termination easier to see and accidental infinite work harder to write.

The example chooses loop because the end condition is written inside the body. count starts at zero, increases once per pass, and when it reaches three, break count exits with the value 3. That value becomes answer. A bare break would yield (), so the type of answer depends on what every possible exit produces. This is a loop expression, not just a repeated statement.

For a known sequence, for usually says more with less code: it asks an iterator for the next item and stops when there are none. While repeats while its boolean condition remains true; it is useful when the condition itself is the central idea. An unconditional loop makes sense when the body must inspect data before deciding to stop, but every path through it should have a comprehensible exit plan. continue jumps to the next pass without running the remainder of the current body.

Trace count on paper for each iteration and mark exactly where the break happens. Then rewrite a three-pass task with for index in 0..3 and compare the two versions. If you remove the break from the original loop, ask whether the program can ever finish. The most readable loop is the one whose termination rule a reader can see immediately.

When choosing a loop form, ask whether the collection owns the elements after iteration. Iterating over `&items` borrows; iterating over `items` can move its elements. Try both and inspect whether the original collection is still available after the loop.

Choose a loop based on what controls repetition. A `for` loop is natural when you already have a range or collection to traverse. A `while` loop repeats while a condition stays true. A plain `loop` continues until a `break` or other exit. Whichever form you choose, identify the state that changes and the condition that eventually stops the work. An accidental infinite loop is usually a missing state update or a boundary that can never be reached.

Trace the example for the first three iterations in a table: counter before, condition, body effect, counter after. Then test an empty input and a one-item input. If you need both position and value, `enumerate()` often reads better than manual indexing. A `break` can also return a value from `loop`; a `continue` skips to the next iteration. Use each only when it makes the exit path easier to see.
writing.feedback: A value after break becomes the value produced by the loop expression.
writing.question: What is stored in value?
writing.rule: Prefer for for iteration; use loop when break defines the exit.
writing.success: Each loop has a visible reason to stop and prints the expected count.
writing.summary: Choose the loop form that states why repetition ends.
writing.task: Use loop with a valued break, then rewrite a fixed pass as for.

writing.exampleCaption: The annotation tells parse which numeric type to produce.
writing.explanation:
parse is generic: the destination type tells it what grammar to use. Because arbitrary text may be invalid, the result is `Result` rather than a bare value. A type annotation or turbofish such as parse::<`i32`>() resolves the target type, after which match, ?, or another deliberate policy handles failure.

Text arrives as bytes and characters, not as a trusted number. The call "42".parse::<`i32`>() asks Rust to interpret it using `i32`'s parsing rules. That operation can fail, so it returns `Result`<`i32`, ParseIntError>. The annotation `Result`<`i32`, _> in the example gives rustc enough information to infer the error type; the underscore does not mean the error disappears. A successful parse produces `Ok`(42), while invalid text such as "forty-two" produces `Err` with diagnostic information.

The match in the example deliberately handles both outcomes. It prints the number on success and the error on failure. In a larger function, ? can propagate an error when the surrounding return type supports it, but that still represents a failure path the caller must consider. unwrap would panic instead, so use it only when a violated invariant truly means the program cannot continue, not for routine user input.

Before choosing a parser, decide the target type and valid range. Parsing "300" as `u8` fails even though the text is made of digits, because 300 is outside that type's range. Try valid, malformed, and out-of-range strings, then record which branch runs for each. A good parser does not just extract a value; it makes invalid input visible at the boundary.

Separate syntax errors from domain errors. The text `-3` may parse successfully as an integer but still be invalid for a positive count. Validate both steps, and return a message that tells the caller which rule was violated.

Text from a user or file is not yet a number, even if it looks like digits. `parse::<i32>()` attempts to turn a `&str` into a typed value and returns `Result`, because the text may be empty, contain letters, or exceed the type's range. The successful branch contains the number; the error branch tells you that the conversion failed. Do not call `unwrap()` on unpredictable input unless a crash is genuinely your intended response.

Try the strings `"42"`, `"-3"`, `"abc"`, and a number too large for `i32`. Predict which parse calls succeed. Then handle both `Ok` and `Err` with `match` and give a reader a useful message for invalid input. If whitespace is allowed by your interface, decide whether to trim it before parsing. Parsing is a boundary: after it succeeds, later code can rely on the value's type rather than repeatedly checking the original text.

answers: fn show(text: &str)
fn show(mut text: String)
fn show(text: Box<String>)
writing.exampleCaption: length borrows text, so main can print it again.
writing.explanation:
The & symbol creates a borrow. A shared reference such as `&str` permits reading but not mutation, and it does not own the value it points to. Passing a reference avoids a move, so the original binding remains usable after the call. Later ownership lessons add the precise aliasing rules and mutable references.

In the example, name owns a `String`. Passing &name to length creates a shared borrow, and the parameter text: `&str` lets the function read the bytes through that borrow. length returns a `usize`, not the text itself. After the call ends, main still owns name and can print it. No second owned `String` had to be made for this read-only question.

A reference is valid only while the value it refers to is available. Rust checks that relationship so code cannot keep a pointer into a value that has already gone away. Shared references permit reading; mutation through a shared reference is not allowed. That is why a function that only needs to inspect text should often accept `&str` instead of taking `String` ownership. It can then work with both owned strings and borrowed string slices supplied by callers.

Borrowing is not a promise that the data will never change anywhere. It is a controlled access rule for a particular period and reference. Later lessons introduce mutable borrows and the rule that prevents conflicting simultaneous access. For now, change length to take `String` by value and see why the owner is unavailable after the call. Restore `&str` and explain what the ampersand changed about the function's contract.

References also have lifetimes, although the compiler often infers them in simple cases. A reference cannot outlive the value it points to. Return owned data or borrow from an input that lives long enough; do not try to return a reference to a local temporary.

A reference lets code temporarily use a value without becoming its owner. If a function accepts `&String` or `&str` to read text, the caller retains the original value after the call. The borrow must remain valid while the reference is used, and a shared borrow does not permit mutation of that value through the same reference. This is easier to understand if you draw two names: the owning binding and the temporary reference pointing to it.

Trace the example at the call site: who owns the string before the call, what the function can read, and who owns it afterward. Replace the borrowed parameter with an owned `String` and observe whether the caller can still use its binding. Then restore the reference. Prefer `&str` for a read-only text parameter when both string literals and `String` values should work. The signature says what the function needs; the borrow checker enforces that promise.
writing.feedback: Borrowing `&str` lets show read the text without taking its `String` owner.
writing.question: What signature keeps name usable?
writing.rule: &T borrows T for read-only use without transferring ownership.
writing.success: The caller retains ownership and no clone is needed.
writing.summary: A shared reference lets a function read a value while the caller keeps ownership.

answers: len borrows self rather than consuming it
usize restores the String
All methods copy their receiver
writing.exampleCaption: trim borrows; to_uppercase creates a new owned `String`.
writing.explanation:
A method call uses dot syntax, and Rust automatically borrows or dereferences the receiver when the signature makes that unambiguous. Chaining is readable when each step produces the value the next step expects. Watch ownership: some methods borrow the receiver, while others consume it and return a new value.

Start at the receiver, the value to the left of the dot. In `name.trim()`, `trim` borrows the string and returns a slice (`&str`) of its contents; it does not edit `name`. The next call, `to_uppercase()`, reads that slice and creates a new `String`. You can still print the original value after both calls. A chain is easiest to reason about when you can name the type after each step: `String` → `&str` → `String`.

Method syntax is a convenient way to pass the receiver as the first argument. `text.len()` and `str::len(text)` express closely related calls; the dot form also lets Rust apply an unambiguous borrow or dereference. It does not erase ownership rules. A method declared with `self` takes the receiver by value; one with `&self` only reads it; one with `&mut self` may modify it. When a value seems to disappear after a method call, inspect that signature before inserting a clone.

For practice, write the chain as separate bindings: `let trimmed = name.trim(); let upper = trimmed.to_uppercase();`. Print all three values and predict which ones own their bytes. Then change a mutable string with `push_str` and compare that in-place edit with making a new uppercase string. Prefer a short chain when each conversion is obvious; use named intermediate values when you need to inspect a failure, annotate a type, or explain the transformation to a teammate.

A method call is still a function call with an explicit receiver. `value.len()` reads as an operation associated with `value`; in an `impl` block, the receiver is commonly written `&self`, `&mut self`, or `self`. These forms mean borrow for reading, borrow for mutation, or take ownership. The receiver choice determines what the caller may do with the value afterward, so read it as part of the method's contract.

Call one read-only method twice on the same value and predict why both calls work. Then write or inspect a method that takes `self` and try to reuse the old binding afterward. A compiler error here is about ownership, not about the dot syntax. Methods can return values, mutate state, or do I/O; the dot alone does not tell you which. Look at the signature and name together. Prefer short methods that preserve a clear invariant over a large chain whose intermediate effects are hard to see.
writing.feedback: The receiver is &self, so the method reads through a temporary borrow.
writing.question: Why is text still usable after `len()`?
writing.rule: Read a method's self parameter to learn its ownership effect.
writing.success: You can tell whether each receiver is borrowed or consumed.
writing.summary: Method syntax puts an operation beside the value it acts on.

answers: Invalid external text is an expected possibility
Result parses faster
Integers can only be returned inside Result
writing.exampleCaption: The caller chooses what an invalid number means for this program.
writing.explanation:
A function returning `Result`<T, E> makes callers handle both success and failure. match is the clearest first tool because both branches stay visible. The ? operator becomes useful once a surrounding function also returns a compatible `Result`. panic and expect are better reserved for broken invariants or controlled examples, not routine bad input.

Imagine a command that reads a port number. The user typing letters is not a broken program; it is an expected input that deserves a useful message and another attempt. `Result<T, E>` makes that distinction part of the function contract. `Ok(value)` contains the value to continue with, while `Err(error)` contains the reason to show, log, or transform. The caller gets to decide whether to retry, choose a default, or stop that operation.

In the example, `parse::<i32>()` returns a `Result`. `map_err` converts the parsing error into a message the API promises to return. The `?` operator takes the number from `Ok`, but returns early from `half` on `Err`. It is not a general shortcut for ignoring a failure: the enclosing function must be able to return a compatible error type. Write a `match` first if the two paths are unfamiliar; once both branches are clear, `?` keeps the successful path readable.

Avoid `unwrap()` on input you do not control. A panic reports a programming defect or a deliberately impossible state; it is a poor response to ordinary bad text. As a small exercise, call `half("12")` and `half("twelve")`, printing the successful answer and an actionable error. Then decide whether dividing an odd integer by two should truncate or be rejected. That is a product rule, and the function signature and tests should make the choice visible.

An error message should be useful at the boundary where it is displayed. Deep inside a reusable parser, preserve a structured error when possible; at the UI boundary, add the input context and a concrete suggestion for correction.

A recoverable error is an outcome your caller may need to handle. `Result<T, E>` contains either `Ok(T)` or `Err(E)`, and the type makes both possibilities visible. The `?` operator returns early from the current function when it sees an `Err`; it is concise propagation, not a way to ignore failure. The surrounding function must have a compatible return type. Use `match` when the current layer can make a meaningful decision, such as asking for another input or choosing a fallback.

Trace the example twice: once with valid input and once with invalid input. Mark the first operation that can fail and whether later lines run. Add a message that tells the user what to fix rather than merely printing a debug dump. Avoid `unwrap()` for normal bad input; reserve it for an invariant you can justify or a deliberate experiment. A good error path leaves the program in a known state and gives the next layer enough context to respond.
writing.feedback: Let the caller decide how to recover instead of forcing a panic.
writing.question: Why is `Result` a better return type here?
writing.rule: Use `Result` for failure the caller can reasonably respond to.
writing.success: Bad text produces a normal error value, not a panic.
writing.summary: `Result` keeps expected failure in the function's type instead of turning it into a crash.
writing.task: Return a descriptive `Result` for invalid input and handle it at the caller.

writing.exampleCaption: Borrowing lets `dbg!` inspect the `Vec` without consuming it.
writing.explanation:
The {:?} formatter uses the `Debug` trait. `dbg!` prints the expression, source location, and value to stderr, then returns the value unchanged. Borrow with `dbg!`(&value) when you want to inspect an owned value without moving it. Remove noisy probes or replace them with deliberate logging before shipping.

A useful debug probe answers a specific question. Before running the program, predict the value at a boundary: after parsing, before a branch, or after a collection update. Put `dbg!` there, run the smallest input that exposes the issue, and compare the printed value with the prediction. If the value is already wrong, move the probe earlier; if it is right, move it later. This narrows the search instead of filling the terminal with unrelated output.

`println!` writes to standard output, which users or another program may be reading as the result. `dbg!` writes to standard error and includes the source expression and location, so it is better suited to a temporary inspection. The macro returns the value it receives. For an owned `String` or `Vec`, passing the value can move it into the macro; pass `&value` to inspect without giving it away. `{:?}` requires `Debug`, and a struct can usually obtain that trait with `#[derive(Debug)]`.

Try the lesson's `name` example twice: first observe the move error, then change the probe to `dbg!(&name)` and run it again. Record what appeared on stderr and what remained on stdout. After finding the cause, remove the probe or replace it with intentional diagnostics that have a stable purpose. A good debugging habit includes a final clean run, because experimental output should not become an accidental part of the program's interface.

`Debug` output helps inspect a running program, but it is not automatically an explanation. Print the value immediately before the branch or calculation you distrust, state what you expected, and compare. `{:?}` uses the `Debug` trait and often exposes structure; `{}` uses `Display` when a user-facing representation exists. An added print can change timing, especially around concurrency, so it is evidence rather than a proof that every execution behaves the same way.

Choose one wrong result in a small example. Write a hypothesis before adding a print, then place exactly one observation that could confirm or refute it. Remove or gate temporary diagnostics once the issue is understood. For a persistent behavior, write a test for the input that failed. If the compiler rejects a value because it lacks `Debug`, derive or implement that trait only when exposing its fields is appropriate. This turns debugging into a sequence of questions rather than a flood of logs.

writing.exampleCaption: In a library crate named lesson_docs, `cargo test` compiles and runs this example.
writing.explanation:
/// documents the item that follows and //! documents the enclosing module or crate. Code blocks inside doc comments are compiled and executed by `cargo test`, so an example that drifts out of date fails the build instead of quietly misleading the next reader.

Comments are most useful when they preserve a reason the code alone cannot show. `//` is suitable for a local decision, such as why a limit exists or why a case is skipped. Repeating the next expression in English makes the reader maintain two copies of the same fact. If the code needs a long explanation of what it does, first see whether clearer names or a smaller function would help.

Documentation comments have a different audience. Place `///` immediately before an item to explain its purpose, parameters, return value, and conditions that matter to callers. Use `//!` for an overview of the containing module or crate. A short example makes the contract concrete: it should demonstrate a representative call and assert the expected result. In a Cargo project, `cargo test` runs valid Rust code blocks in documentation as doctests. A doctest is compiled separately, so it must import the documented public item through the crate's actual name or otherwise define everything it uses. A bare call to a library function without an import can fail even when the function itself is correct.

For the practice snippet, the assertion expects five while the function returns four. Predict the failure before running it, then fix the expectation and add an edge case such as zero. Keep an example short enough that a reader can verify the claim at a glance. If an example needs setup, hide only incidental setup lines with rustdoc's `#` marker; do not hide the behaviour being taught. Treat doc failures as feedback that either code or its promised behaviour changed.

In a published crate, write the actual crate import in the example so the doctest exercises the public function instead of a copy of its logic. Run the test after renaming an API as well as after changing its result.

A comment should explain a decision the code cannot show, such as why a boundary is excluded or why a particular failure is safe to retry. Restating `count += 1` as 'increment count' adds little. Rust doc comments beginning with `///` attach documentation to an item, and fenced Rust examples in documentation can be compiled and tested by `cargo test` in a suitable crate. That lets an API example fail visibly when the API changes.

Write one doc comment for a small public function: what it returns, what happens on invalid input, and a short example using the actual crate path. Run its documentation test. Then deliberately change the function signature and see the example fail until you update it. Use ordinary `//` comments for local reasoning and reserve `///` for the contract readers need at the API boundary. Keep examples small enough that someone can copy them without guessing missing imports.
writing.feedback: Doc examples are compiled and asserted, so a wrong example is a failing test.
writing.question: What happens when you run `cargo test` on that?
writing.rule: A doc example is a test, so documentation cannot silently rot.
writing.success: The example states the behaviour and would fail if the code changed.
writing.summary: Doc comments are compiled, and their examples are run as tests.

self consumes the counter, so it cannot be used again
It should return Self so the call can be chained
writing.exampleCaption: &self borrows, so the caller keeps ownership.
writing.explanation:
`impl` blocks attach constructors and methods to the type. The receiver spells out the ownership contract: self consumes the value, &self borrows it for reading, and &`mut` self borrows it for modification — so a method signature tells you what it will do before you read the body.

A struct groups values that belong to one concept. `Rectangle { width, height }` gives those numbers names, so the caller cannot silently confuse the two positions in a tuple. Choose field types that express the valid domain; unsigned dimensions reject negative values at the type level, though you still need to think about multiplication overflow for very large inputs. Construct one value, print its area, then change only its width to see how the named fields clarify the operation.

An `impl` block puts operations next to the type they describe. An associated function such as `Rectangle::new(width, height)` has no `self` receiver and can validate input during construction. A method such as `area(&self)` borrows an existing rectangle. This means several read-only calls can share the same value. A mutating method uses `&mut self` and requires a mutable receiver; a consuming method uses `self` and leaves the old binding unavailable afterward. The signature is a compact ownership contract for callers.

In the counter practice snippet, `bump(self)` consumes the counter and returns only a number. That could be deliberate for a one-shot conversion, but it is surprising for an operation named "bump." If the goal is to retain and update the counter, use `fn bump(&mut self)` and increment its field; if the goal is to produce a modified copy, return a new `Counter` and name the method accordingly. Decide the desired post-call state first, then choose the receiver. This habit prevents ownership errors from turning into unnecessary clones.

A struct combines fields that belong to one concept. A `User` with `name` and `age` is easier to understand than two unrelated variables passed together through many functions. The field names describe roles; the type groups them into one value. Constructing a struct requires values for every required field unless a constructor or default supplies them. Access a field with dot syntax, and make the binding mutable if you intend to change a field through it.

Trace a value from construction to a function call: which code owns it, which fields are read, and whether it can still be used afterward. Then add a field and follow the compiler errors at each construction site; they show where your data model is used. If a field must never be invalid, consider a constructor that validates it and keeps the raw fields private. lessons.title: Enums & Match

answers: Nothing — a wildcard arm keeps the match exhaustive
A new variant silently falls into it instead of erroring
It makes the match slower by adding a runtime check
writing.exampleCaption: Adding a variant breaks every match that does not handle it.
writing.explanation:
match forces every variant to be handled, so adding a new state turns every incomplete match into a compile error instead of a silent bug. Variants can carry data, which lets one type model a whole state machine rather than a bag of loosely related fields.

A boolean can distinguish two states, but it becomes obscure when a feature has several states or each state carries different data. An enum names the alternatives. `Message::Quit` carries nothing, `Message::Move` carries two coordinates, and `Message::Write` carries text. A value is exactly one variant at a time, so code cannot accidentally pair coordinates with a quit message as it might with a loose struct of optional fields.

A `match` examines the variant and binds only the data available in that branch. Every arm must produce a compatible type if the match is used as an expression. The compiler's exhaustiveness check is valuable during maintenance: adding `Message::Resize` points to every decision that now needs a policy. A wildcard `_` can be appropriate when all remaining cases truly share the same behavior, but it hides newly added variants if used merely to silence the compiler. For a small state machine, spell out the known cases.

Trace the sample with one value of each variant. Note that `Message::Write(t)` moves its `String` out when the enum is matched by value; match a reference, `match &message`, if you need to keep the original message. Then add a variant with a field and update the rendering match explicitly. This exercise connects data modeling, exhaustive control flow, and ownership. A well-shaped enum makes invalid combinations harder to represent and changes to the model easier to audit.

When the enum is public, adding a variant may require downstream users to update their exhaustive matches. That compile-time interruption is useful: it forces every caller to consider the new state rather than silently treating it as an old one.

An enum is one value chosen from several named variants. A variant can carry data, so `Message::Text(String)` and `Message::Quit` have different shapes under one type. A `match` can handle each shape explicitly. The compiler checks that every possible variant is covered unless you use a wildcard; that guarantee is especially useful when a new variant is added later.

For each variant in the example, write down what data it carries. Then trace a `match`: which arm runs, which fields are bound, and what value the arm produces. Add one new variant and inspect the exhaustiveness error before writing its behavior. Avoid a wildcard when it would hide an important new case. Enums are useful when exactly one state can be active at a time; several independent booleans often allow impossible combinations. Make invalid combinations unrepresentable where the domain rules are stable.
writing.feedback: A catch-all removes the compiler's help exactly when you add a state.
writing.question: What does the wildcard cost you?
writing.rule: match is exhaustive: every variant must be handled.
writing.success: The match is exhaustive without a wildcard hiding a case.
writing.summary: Enums model a value that is exactly one of several variants.
writing.task: Define a message enum and render every variant with match.
